An undertaker is a person whose profession is to manage everything that needs to happen when someone dies — particularly preparing the dead body and organizing the funeral. In simple terms, they are the professional who takes care of the deceased and helps the surviving family through the entire process of saying goodbye.

An undertaker's work involves several distinct responsibilities:

Collecting and preparing the body
When a person dies, the undertaker collects the body — often from a hospital, home, or the place of death — and brings it to their establishment. They then prepare it. This preparation can include:

  • Embalming — a process of preserving and chemically treating the body to slow decomposition, especially if there is going to be a public viewing or if burial is days away.
  • Restoration — making the body look peaceful and presentable. This includes cleaning, dressing the body in clothes (often provided by the family), and applying cosmetics to give the person a natural appearance.
  • Refrigeration — keeping the body preserved in a cool environment until the funeral.

Arranging and managing the funeral
This is the deeply practical and organizational side of their job. They:

  • Meet with the grieving family to understand and plan what they want
  • Arrange the venue and time of the funeral service
  • Coordinate with clergy, religious leaders, or civil celebrants if needed
  • Organize the coffin or casket (and help the family choose one)
  • Handle all official paperwork, including death certificates, burial permits, and other legal documents
  • Arrange transportation of the body to the place of worship, the funeral home, the cemetery, or the crematorium
  • Manage the actual ceremony on the day — directing staff, managing the schedule, ensuring everything runs smoothly

Final disposition
The undertaker oversees the final step — either burial in a cemetery or cremation. They coordinate with cemeteries, arrange grave plots, and in the case of cremation, handle the crematorium and return the ashes (also called "cremated remains" or "cremains") to the family.

An undertaker works out of a place called a funeral home, funeral parlour, or funeral parlour (the British spelling). This is a business premises specifically designed for this purpose. It typically has a reception area where the undertaker meets families, preparation rooms where bodies are handled, and chapels or viewing rooms where families can see the body before the funeral.

The word comes directly from the verb "to undertake", which means to take on a task or responsibility. An undertaker is literally a person who undertakes (takes on) the task of a funeral. This is important to understand because it also unlocks an older, broader sense of the word (explained below).

In earlier English — roughly the 16th through 19th centuries — "undertaker" was used in a much wider sense: any person who undertakes (commits to carrying out) any task, project, or enterprise on behalf of others, often for payment or profit.

Under this meaning, a merchant who contracted to supply goods to an army could be called an undertaker. A builder who took on a large construction project was an undertaker. Even a legal agent who took on a case could be described this way.

This general meaning is now almost entirely obsolete in everyday English. If you encounter it in older literature or historical texts, you should read it in this broader sense — not necessarily in connection with funerals.

Two specific historical uses worth knowing:

  1. England, early 17th century: "Undertakers" referred to certain politicians in the English Parliament who undertook (promised the King) that they could manage and control Parliament on his behalf — essentially political brokers or deal-makers between the Crown and Parliament.
  2. Plantation of Ulster, Ireland, 17th century: English and Scottish settlers who were given confiscated Irish land were called "undertakers" because they had undertaken (formally promised) to settle the land with Protestant settlers and abide by certain conditions.

These are specialized historical uses. Unless you are reading historical texts from these periods, you will rarely encounter them.

These three words all refer to roughly the same profession, but with nuances:

  • Undertaker — the traditional English word, used for centuries. Still widely understood and used in everyday speech, especially in British English.
  • Funeral director — the more modern, professional title now preferred in most Western countries, particularly in formal or business contexts. It reflects the managerial and organizational side of the job, and many in the profession prefer it as it sounds more dignified and professional than "undertaker."
  • Mortician — a term used mainly in American English. It emphasizes the technical, body-preparation side of the work (from mortis, relating to death). A mortician may also be a licensed embalmer.

In practice, these terms are often used interchangeably, though the preferred title varies by country and context.

The word "undertaker" occasionally appears in figurative language, meaning anyone who takes charge of a difficult, grim, or concluding matter — someone who "buries" things, whether literally or metaphorically. This is a loose, informal usage drawn from the funeral association.

In popular culture, "The Undertaker" is the ring name of a famous American professional wrestling character — a deliberately dramatic, death-themed persona that uses the funeral imagery of the word for effect.

UseMeaning

To put it plainly:

  • In modern everyday use: An undertaker is the professional who manages funerals — collecting and preparing dead bodies, arranging and running funeral services, handling all paperwork, and overseeing burial or cremation.
  • In older English (now rare): Any person who formally takes on a task, project, or enterprise on behalf of others.
  • In specific historical contexts: Political deal-makers or colonial settlers who made formal promises or undertook contracts.

The modern funeral-related meaning is by far the most important one to know. If someone says "the undertaker," they almost certainly mean the funeral professional.
